  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();

<article class="ltx_document">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">On the Adversarial Robustness of Discrete Image Tokenizers</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Rishika Bhagwatkar
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">

<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Irina Rish
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Discrete image tokenizers encode visual inputs as sequences of tokens from a finite vocabulary and are gaining popularity in multimodal systems, including encoder-only, encoder-decoder, and decoder-only models. However, unlike CLIP encoders, their vulnerability to adversarial attacks has not been explored. Ours being the first work studying this topic, we first formulate attacks that aim to perturb the features extracted by discrete tokenizers, and thus change the extracted tokens. These attacks are computationally efficient, application-agnostic, and effective across classification, multimodal retrieval, and captioning tasks. Second, to defend against this vulnerability, inspired by recent work on robust CLIP encoders, we fine-tune popular tokenizers with unsupervised adversarial training, keeping all other components frozen. While unsupervised and task-agnostic, our approach significantly improves robustness to both unsupervised and end-to-end supervised attacks and generalizes well to unseen tasks and data. Unlike supervised adversarial training, our approach can leverage unlabeled images, making it more versatile. Overall, our work highlights the critical role of tokenizer robustness in downstream tasks and presents an important step in the development of safe multimodal foundation models.
<a href="https://robust-tokenizers.github.io/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">

<span class="ltx_inline-block fas fa-globe" aria-hidden="true">
</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">robust-tokenizers.github.io</span>
</a></p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_keywords">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_keywords">Keywords: </h6>Machine Learning, ICML
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Similar to text tokenizers, discrete image tokenizers represent visual input as a sequence, typically of fixed length, of vectors from a finite codebook <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Van Den Oord et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2024b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bachmann et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
However, unlike text tokenizers such as BPE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gage, 1994</a>)</cite>, they rely on deep networks trained alongside a de-tokenization model for image reconstruction.
These de-tokenizers enable synthetic image generation in autoregressive frameworks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, which are competitive with diffusion models.
Recently, discrete image tokenizers have become integral to complex architectures as image encoders, offering a popular alternative to CLIP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Radford et al., 2021</a>)</cite> and DINO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Oquab et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.
Multimodal encoder-decoder models such as Unified-IO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lu et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, 4M <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mizrahi et al., 2023</a>)</cite> and 4M-21 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bachmann et al., 2024</a>)</cite> employ discrete tokenizers for natural images and segmentation maps, while FuseLIP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schlarmann et al., 2025</a>)</cite> combines them with early-fusion in text-image models trained with contrastive objectives.
These models can be applied to various unimodal and multimodal tasks, including classification, retrieval, and VQA.
Additionally, decoder-only generative models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chameleon Team, 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al., 2025</a>)</cite> leverage discrete tokenizers for unified vision and language understanding and generation. Consequently, the robustness of image tokenizers to adversarial attacks directly impacts the vulnerability of all models using them.
While much research has focused on improving the adversarial robustness of standard encoders (e.g., CLIP), this aspect of discrete image tokenizers remains completely unexplored.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we first study the vulnerability of recently proposed discrete image tokenizers, both in isolation and as part of larger models.
In particular, we test <span id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">unsupervised attacks</span> which aim to alter the tokenization of the original image by distorting the encoding and consequently assigning incorrect codebook vectors.
Since these attacks target only the discrete image tokenizer, the resulting perturbations are agnostic to the downstream tasks for which the tokens are used (e.g., reconstruction, classification, language generation).
We show that such direct unsupervised attacks are often effective against standard tokenizers, and in some cases even competitive with end-to-end supervised attacks which require task-specific information (e.g., labels) and are more computationally expensive because they target the entire system.
For instance, in autoregressive multimodal models, the large language model (LLM) has one to two orders of magnitude more parameters than the image tokenizer.
Notably, our unsupervised attacks can make an LLM output a target (malicious) caption for a given input image by matching its tokenization to that of a target image semantically aligned with the desired caption, without requiring direct access to the LLM itself.
These results highlight the vulnerability of existing discrete image tokenizers, and the safety risks they pose to downstream models across tasks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Then, in order to mitigate this vulnerability, we extend the framework of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schlarmann et al. (2024)</a></cite>, introduced for robust CLIP vision encoders, to discrete image tokenizers.
In particular, we fine-tune discrete image tokenizers with unsupervised adversarial training, i.e., we train the model to yield consistent tokenization for the original images and their corresponding adversarial counterparts, computed on-the-fly by unsupervised attacks.
Since this approach is independent of any downstream task, the resulting tokenizer can be directly plugged back into any system that relied on the original tokenizer without the need for additional adaptations.
In fact, through extensive experiments, we show that unsupervised adversarial fine-tuning increases the robustness to end-to-end supervised attacks in a variety of tasks, from image classification to captioning.
By fine-tuning TiTok tokenizers, we obtain robust FuseLIP models for multimodal embedding, while with adversarial training of UniTok we get a multimodal LLM (MLLM) robust on VQA and captioning tasks.
Finally, we provide fine-grained analyses of the effect of unsupervised attacks by reconstructing the adversarial images, which reveal quite significant differences across tokenizers, supervised vs. unsupervised adversarial training, and the role of the dataset used for adversarial fine-tuning.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Contributions.</span> In summary, (a) our work is the first to systematically test and improve the adversarial robustness of discrete image tokenizers. (b) To evaluate their vulnerability, we propose unsupervised attacks that are both efficient and task-agnostic. (c) Importantly, we also show that the same attacks can be leveraged to adversarially fine-tune these tokenizers. (d) Our unsupervised adversarial fine-tuning robustifies the tokenizers against both unsupervised and end-to-end supervised attacks, at a significantly lower computational cost than end-to-end supervised adversarial fine-tuning. (e) In contrast to supervised defenses, our defense can directly leverage any amount of unlabeled data. (f) These robust tokenizers can be seamlessly integrated as image encoders in larger systems, strengthening the robustness of multimodal embedding models (FuseLIP) and MLLMs (UniTok-MLLM) to all attacks (supervised or not) across diverse tasks well beyond the training data.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Image tokenizers.</span>
Image tokenizers aim to compress visual data via deep learning models, trained with image reconstruction objectives possibly aided by auxiliary losses.
Continuous tokenizers encode images into a continuous feature space <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fan et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
Conversely, discrete tokenizers convert images into sequences of tokens drawn from a fixed vocabulary, typically via vector quantization.
VQ-VAE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Van Den Oord et al., 2017</a>)</cite> introduced a vector-quantized bottleneck, replacing continuous latents with discrete codes,
later improved and extended by several works <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2024a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mentzer et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
While early methods encode images into 2D grids of latents, recent works have developed 1D tokenizers that return a sequence of tokens without spatial structure <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2024b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Miwa et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bachmann et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
TiTok <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2024b</a>)</cite> demonstrates that as few as 32 tokens can produce high-quality reconstructions.
UniTok <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al., 2025</a>)</cite> improves generalization in generative and discriminative tasks by introducing multi-codebook quantization while integrating reconstruction and CLIP supervision. Other approaches, such as One-D-Piece <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Miwa et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and FlexTok <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bachmann et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, allow varying the number of tokens to balance compression and reconstruction quality at inference.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18252v1/pl_sup_unsup_imagenette_v2.svg" id="S2.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:429/108;" width="429" height="108"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S2.F1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Unsupervised vs supervised adversarial attacks for classification.<span id="S2.F1.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">
We report the robust accuracy when varying the perturbation radius <math id="S2.F1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϵ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math> (scaled to [0, 255]) for three classifiers on Imagenette: TiTok with ViT probing (left), FlexTok with linear probing (middle), and zero-shot UniTok (right).
In most cases, our unsupervised attacks (blue curves), which target only the image tokenizer and do not need label information, perform close to end-to-end supervised attacks (red), which target the entire classifier and use labels. For small <math id="S2.F1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϵ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math>, our unsupervised attacks are slightly worse than the supervised ones.
Both attacks are optimized with 100 iterations of APGD on 500 images.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Adversarial robustness of image encoders.</span>
Adversarial robustness to <math id="S2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{p}</annotation></semantics></math>-bounded attacks has been extensively studied for a variety of vision tasks, such as image classification <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Croce et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, semantic segmentation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Croce et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, object detection <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, with the development of many algorithms to both generate adversarial perturbations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Carlini and Wagner, 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Croce and Hein, 2020</a>)</cite> and improve the robustness to deep learning models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Madry et al., 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2019</a>)</cite>.
With the development of foundation multimodal models such as CLIP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Radford et al., 2021</a>)</cite> and SAM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kirillov et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, those approaches have been adapted to modern scenarios.
Moreover, new techniques have been designed to attack multimodal autoregressive LLMs like LLaVA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024</a>)</cite> by perturbing the input images, which allows an attacker to control the model output <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schlarmann and Hein, 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qi et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
These works reveal the persisting vulnerability of image encoders to adversarial perturbations, both in isolation and when used as part of more complex systems <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bhagwatkar et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
Therefore, a few works have proposed methods to improve their robustness, such as <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mao et al. (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schlarmann et al. (2024)</a></cite> who fine-tuned the vision encoder of CLIP with variants of adversarial training <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Madry et al., 2018</a>)</cite>.
However, to our knowledge, the robustness of discrete image tokenizers has not been studied so far.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Testing and Improving the Adversarial Robustness of Image Tokenizers via Unsupervised Attacks
</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We first provide a background on discrete image tokenizers, then introduce our unsupervised attacks as well as experiments supporting their effectiveness,
and finally discuss how to leverage them to improve the robustness of tokenizers.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Background.</span>
Discrete image tokenizers extract a sequence of <math id="S3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> <math id="S3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional latent vectors from an input image.
Concretely, they first leverage an encoder <math id="S3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi:I\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{T\times d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi:I\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{T\times d}</annotation></semantics></math>, typically a CNN or vision transformer, that maps an image <math id="S3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> embeddings, <math id="S3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\,\phi(x)=\{h_{i}\}_{i=1}^{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\,\phi(x)=\{h_{i}\}_{i=1}^{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Then, a vector quantizer with a learned codebook <math id="S3.p2.m7" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathcal{C}=\{e_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\}_{k=1}^{K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>K</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{C}=\{e_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\}_{k=1}^{K}</annotation></semantics></math> replaces each pre-quantization embedding <math id="S3.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math> (at location <math id="S3.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>) with its nearest code,
i.e., <math id="S3.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{i}=\argmin_{k\in[K]}\left\|h_{i}-e_{k}\right\|_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>min</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></msub><mo>⁡</mo><msub><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{i}=\argmin_{k\in[K]}\left\|h_{i}-e_{k}\right\|_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>.
This yields a discrete index map <math id="S3.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{q_{i}\}_{i=1}^{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>T</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{q_{i}\}_{i=1}^{T}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Unlike continuous encoders that output continuous space embeddings and remain differentiable everywhere, nearest-neighbor quantization is piecewise constant since all embeddings with a particular nearest code are mapped to it, creating discretized cells in the continuous latent space.
Hence, even small shifts at the boundaries of these cells can alter nearest code and index.
Encoder and codebook are learned jointly using straight-through updates.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Unsupervised attacks via embedding distortion</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Pre-trained image tokenizers are used as plug-ins in complex systems for multiple downstream tasks. Therefore, we aim to develop attacks that can be effective regardless of the downstream application.
Since the representation of an image <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> used by any downstream model is determined by the codebook tokens output by the tokenizer, we expect that changing the tokens will lead to an uninformative or distorted encoding of <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>.
While we could aim to directly change the index sequence returned by the tokenizer, the indices themselves carry no (or minimal) semantic or perceptual information, and the resulting problem is not differentiable.
Hence, we propose an attack in the pre-quantization embedding space of discrete image tokenizers.
Specifically, we maximize the <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>-distance between the embeddings of the clean and perturbed images, similar to existing attacks on continuous encoders <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Croce and Hein, 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schlarmann et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, i.e., we aim to solve</p>
<table id="S3.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.E1"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\max_{\left\|\delta\right\|_{p}\leq\epsilon}\;\sum_{i=1}^{T}\left\|h_{i}(x+\delta)-h_{i}(x)\right\|_{2}^{2}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>max</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mmultiscripts><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>T</mi></munderover><mprescripts></mprescripts><mrow><msub><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mi>δ</mi><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>≤</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow><mrow></mrow></mmultiscripts></mstyle><mo>⁡</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\max_{\left\|\delta\right\|_{p}\leq\epsilon}\;\sum_{i=1}^{T}\left\|h_{i}(x+\delta)-h_{i}(x)\right\|_{2}^{2},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{i}(\cdot)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{i}(\cdot)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math> is the <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>-th pre-quantization embedding produced by the image encoder, and <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>δ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta</annotation></semantics></math> is the adversarial perturbation constrained by an <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{p}</annotation></semantics></math>-norm bound <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϵ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math>.
Intuitively, our approach aims to shift the encoder output sufficiently far in latent space to alter the resulting quantized codes, thereby corrupting any downstream application of the tokens.
We remark that our objective directly manipulates the encoder output (prior to vector quantization), without requiring access to the codebook or any information (e.g., class labels) of the downstream applications.</p>
</div>

</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span><span id="S3.F2.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Reconstruction of unsupervised attacks.</span>
For each tokenizer, we show the reconstruction (given by the corresponding de-tokization models) of the clean images and adversarial images computed by unsupervised attacks at <math id="S3.F2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon=\nicefrac{{4}}{{255}},\nicefrac{{8}}{{255}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mpadded voffset="0.3em"><mn mathsize="0.700em">4</mn></mpadded><mpadded style="width:-0.15em;" lspace="-0.1em" width="-0.15em"><mo stretchy="true" symmetric="true">/</mo></mpadded><mn mathsize="0.700em">255</mn></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mpadded voffset="0.3em"><mn mathsize="0.700em">8</mn></mpadded><mpadded style="width:-0.15em;" lspace="-0.1em" width="-0.15em"><mo stretchy="true" symmetric="true">/</mo></mpadded><mn mathsize="0.700em">255</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon=\nicefrac{{4}}{{255}},\nicefrac{{8}}{{255}}</annotation></semantics></math> with 2500 steps of APGD
.
The perturbed inputs affect the reconstruction differently depending on the tokenizer, with TiTok yielding the most distorted decoded images while FlexTok being most robust, with still clearly recognizable subjects.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Effectiveness of unsupervised attacks.</span> To assess the effectiveness of our unsupervised attack, we first compare it to end-to-end supervised attacks on image classification.
We obtain three diverse classifiers based on discrete tokenizers on the Imagenette dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Howard, 2019</a>)</cite>: we train a ViT probe on the quantized features of TiTok-BL128 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>, a linear probe on FlexTok <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bachmann et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, and zero-shot UniTok <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
We compare unsupervised attacks, where APGD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Croce and Hein, 2020</a>)</cite> is used to optimize Eq. (<a href="#S3.E1" title="Equation 1 ‣ 3.1 Unsupervised attacks via embedding distortion ‣ 3 Testing and Improving the Adversarial Robustness of Image Tokenizers via Unsupervised Attacks ‣ On the Adversarial Robustness of Discrete Image Tokenizers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>), to a standard end-to-end attack (APGD on the cross entropy loss) which targets the entire classifier and requires label information, both with 100 iterations.
Fig. <a href="#S2.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ On the Adversarial Robustness of Discrete Image Tokenizers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> shows the robust accuracy of the classifiers when varying the radius <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϵ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math> of the <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{\infty}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{\infty}</annotation></semantics></math>-bounded attacks.
Notably, our unsupervised attacks (blue curves) often perform close to the end-to-end supervised attacks (red), lagging behind particularly for small <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϵ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math> values.
This also shows that even at limited computational cost (only 100 iterations), unsupervised attacks are effective in fooling the classifiers, and hence are useful for adversarial training (see Sec. <a href="#S3" title="3 Testing and Improving the Adversarial Robustness of Image Tokenizers via Unsupervised Attacks ‣ On the Adversarial Robustness of Discrete Image Tokenizers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>).
Finally, we see that the classifiers built on discrete tokenizers are highly vulnerable to adversarial perturbations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Reconstruction of adversarial images.</span>
A unique aspect of our setup is that we can use the image de-tokenizers to reconstruct the adversarial images derived by unsupervised attacks.
We qualitatively estimate how distorting the features extracted by the tokenizer’s encoder impacts the reconstruction.
In Fig. <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.1 Unsupervised attacks via embedding distortion ‣ 3 Testing and Improving the Adversarial Robustness of Image Tokenizers via Unsupervised Attacks ‣ On the Adversarial Robustness of Discrete Image Tokenizers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, we provide several examples of reconstruction of unsupervised attacks (2500 iterations of APGD) at different <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϵ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math>.
Despite these attacks being similarly effective on classification (as mentioned above), they affect reconstruction differently depending on the tokenizer, with TiTok yielding the most distorted reconstructed images while FlexTok being the most robust with still clearly recognizable subjects.
This hints to some structural difference among image tokenization approaches which might impact robustness, presenting an interesting direction for future work.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Robust tokenizers via unsupervised adversarial fine-tuning</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A common approach to improve the robustness of neural networks is adversarial training <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Madry et al., 2018</a>)</cite>, where adversarial perturbations are generated on the fly during training and used to augment the original training set.
In our case, we want to make the image tokenization invariant to adversarial perturbations while preserving its effectiveness for downstream applications.
Inspired by the approach of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schlarmann et al. (2024)</a></cite> for improving the robustness of CLIP’s image encoder, we propose adversarially fine-tuning the image tokenizer on our unsupervised attack.
This yields</p>

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" <td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">as the training objective, where <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> are the parameters of the fine-tuned tokenizer, <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta_{\textrm{orig}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>θ</mi><mtext>orig</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta_{\textrm{orig}}</annotation></semantics></math> the parameters of the original tokenizer (before fine-tuning), and <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}</annotation></semantics></math> is the training dataset.
This loss pushes the fine-tuned tokenizer to yield consistent embeddings in an <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{p}</annotation></semantics></math>-ball of radius <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϵ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math> around the embeddings given by the original tokenizer.
Therefore, the fine-tuned tokenizers could readily replace the original tokenizers in downstream tasks without hurting clean performance while improving robustness.
In principle, the quantization steps of discrete tokenizers make it possible to preserve the downstream performance even without exactly solving Eq. (<a href="#S3.E2" title="Equation 2 ‣ 3.2 Robust tokenizers via unsupervised adversarial fine-tuning ‣ 3 Testing and Improving the Adversarial Robustness of Image Tokenizers via Unsupervised Attacks ‣ On the Adversarial Robustness of Discrete Image Tokenizers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>), since sufficiently close embeddings lead to the same codebook indices.
Compared to task-specific end-to-end supervised adversarial training, our task-agnostic approach has several advantages: <span id="S3.SS2.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(i)</span> it yields tokenizers which can be deployed across multiple downstream applications, <span id="S3.SS2.p1.2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(ii)</span> can leverage virtually any image dataset, even beyond that used for pre-training (as we show in Sec. <a href="#S5" title="5 Additional Analyses ‣ On the Adversarial Robustness of Discrete Image Tokenizers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>) since it does not need label information, and <span id="S3.SS2.p1.2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(iii)</span> fine-tunes only a subset of the parameters, i.e., those of the tokenizer’s encoder, substantially lowering the computational cost (as we show in Sec. <a href="#S5" title="5 Additional Analyses ‣ On the Adversarial Robustness of Discrete Image Tokenizers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experiments</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In the following, we present results for the original and our adversarially fine-tuned tokenizers across tasks and datasets.
In detail, we experiment with two vector-quantized image tokenizers, TiTok-BL128 and UniTok, since both, unlike FlexTok, are part of larger models and can be tested on multiple downstream tasks.
In addition, we report the results of the smaller TiTok-S128 in App. <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Additional Experimental Results ‣ On the Adversarial Robustness of Discrete Image Tokenizers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>.
To obtain the robust versions, we adversarially fine-tune only the encoder of each tokenizer, while keeping the codebook, downstream decoders, LLMs or any other components frozen.
We fine-tune for one epoch under <math id="S4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{\infty}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{\infty}</annotation></semantics></math>-bounded perturbations with our unsupervised embedding-space attack (10 steps of APGD), see Sec. <a href="#S3" title="3 Testing and Improving the Adversarial Robustness of Image Tokenizers via Unsupervised Attacks ‣ On the Adversarial Robustness of Discrete Image Tokenizers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, with perturbation radii <math id="S4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon\in\{\nicefrac{{4}}{{255}},\nicefrac{{8}}{{255}},\nicefrac{{12}}{{255}},\nicefrac{{16}}{{255}}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mrow><mpadded voffset="0.3em"><mn mathsize="0.700em">4</mn></mpadded><mpadded style="width:-0.15em;" lspace="-0.1em" width="-0.15em"><mo stretchy="true" symmetric="true">/</mo></mpadded><mn mathsize="0.700em">255</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mpadded voffset="0.3em"><mn mathsize="0.700em">8</mn></mpadded><mpadded style="width:-0.15em;" lspace="-0.1em" width="-0.15em"><mo stretchy="true" symmetric="true">/</mo></mpadded><mn mathsize="0.700em">255</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mpadded voffset="0.3em"><mn mathsize="0.700em">12</mn></mpadded><mpadded style="width:-0.15em;" lspace="-0.1em" width="-0.15em"><mo stretchy="true" symmetric="true">/</mo></mpadded><mn mathsize="0.700em">255</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mpadded voffset="0.3em"><mn mathsize="0.700em">16</mn></mpadded><mpadded style="width:-0.15em;" lspace="-0.1em" width="-0.15em"><mo stretchy="true" symmetric="true">/</mo></mpadded><mn mathsize="0.700em">255</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon\in\{\nicefrac{{4}}{{255}},\nicefrac{{8}}{{255}},\nicefrac{{12}}{{255}},\nicefrac{{16}}{{255}}\}</annotation></semantics></math>, on ImageNet-1k.
More details on the setup are in App. <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Experimental Details ‣ On the Adversarial Robustness of Discrete Image Tokenizers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>.
Remarkably, despite adversarially fine-tuning only on ImageNet-1k, the resulting robust tokenizers exhibit strong robustness across a wide range of downstream datasets and tasks, highlighting their ability to transfer robustness beyond the training domain.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span><span id="S4.T1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Evaluation of FuseLIP on image classification and multimodal retrieval.</span> We report the clean and robust accuracy (%) under <math id="S4.T1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{\infty}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{\infty}</annotation></semantics></math>-bounded perturbations with <math id="S4.T1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon\in\{2/255,4/255\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.110em" minsize="1.110em">{</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>255</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>255</mn></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.110em" minsize="1.110em">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon\in\{2/255,4/255\}</annotation></semantics></math> for original and robust tokenizers trained on different radii. </figcaption>

<td id="S4.T1.9.4.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_r" style="padding-left:4.5pt;padding-right:4.5pt;"><math id="S4.T1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{AT}^{\nicefrac{{4}}{{255}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mtext mathsize="0.900em">AT</mtext><mrow><mpadded voffset="0.3em"><mn mathsize="0.640em">4</mn></mpadded><mpadded style="width:-0.15em;" lspace="-0.1em" width="-0.15em"><mo stretchy="true" symmetric="true">/</mo></mpadded><mn mathsize="0.640em">255</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{AT}^{\nicefrac{{4}}{{255}}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>

<td id="S4.T3.9.6.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding-left:6.5pt;padding-right:6.5pt;"><span id="S4.T3.9.6.6.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">39.4</span></td>
<td id="S4.T3.9.6.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_r" style="padding-left:6.5pt;padding-right:6.5pt;"><span id="S4.T3.9.6.7.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">33.9</span></td>
<td id="S4.T3.9.6.8" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding-left:6.5pt;padding-right:6.5pt;"><span id="S4.T3.9.6.8.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">64.2</span></td>
<td id="S4.T3.9.6.9" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding-left:6.5pt;padding-right:6.5pt;"><span id="S4.T3.9.6.9.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">49.4</span></td>
<td id="S4.T3.9.6.10" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_r" style="padding-left:6.5pt;padding-right:6.5pt;"><span id="S4.T3.9.6.10.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">40.2</span></td>
<td id="S4.T3.9.6.11" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding-left:6.5pt;padding-right:6.5pt;"><span id="S4.T3.9.6.11.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">57.5</span></td>
<td id="S4.T3.9.6.12" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding-left:6.5pt;padding-right:6.5pt;"><span id="S4.T3.9.6.12.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">47.0</span></td>
<td id="S4.T3.9.6.13" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center" style="padding-left:6.5pt;padding-right:6.5pt;"><span id="S4.T3.9.6.13.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">40.0</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S4.T3.9.7" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.T3.9.7.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb ltx_border_r" style="padding-left:6.5pt;padding-right:6.5pt;"><math id="S4.T3.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{AT}^{\nicefrac{{16}}{{255}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mtext mathsize="0.900em">AT</mtext><mrow><mpadded voffset="0.3em"><mn mathsize="0.640em">16</mn></mpadded><mpadded style="width:-0.15em;" lspace="-0.1em" width="-0.15em"><mo stretchy="true" symmetric="true">/</mo></mpadded><mn mathsize="0.640em">255</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{AT}^{\nicefrac{{16}}{{255}}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td id="S4.T3.9.7.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:6.5pt;padding-right:6.5pt;"><span id="S4.T3.9.7.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">57.5</span></td>
<td id="S4.T3.9.7.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:6.5pt;padding-right:6.5pt;"><span id="S4.T3.9.7.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">49.7</span></td>
<td id="S4.T3.9.7.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_r" style="padding-left:6.5pt;padding-right:6.5pt;"><span id="S4.T3.9.7.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">43.7</span></td>
<td id="S4.T3.9.7.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:6.5pt;padding-right:6.5pt;"><span id="S4.T3.9.7.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">45.1</span></td>
<td id="S4.T3.9.7.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:6.5pt;padding-right:6.5pt;"><span id="S4.T3.9.7.6.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">38.8</span></td>
<td id="S4.T3.9.7.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_r" style="padding-left:6.5pt;padding-right:6.5pt;"><span id="S4.T3.9.7.7.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">32.2</span></td>
