<td id="S4.T3.9.7.13" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:6.5pt;padding-right:6.5pt;"><span id="S4.T3.9.7.13.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">38.6</span></td></tr>
</table>
</figure>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Robust tokenizers lead to robust embedding models
</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">First, we test the effect of replacing the original tokenizer’s encoder with our adversarially fine-tuned version in embedding models, for classification and multimodal retrieval.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">FuseLIP.</span>
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schlarmann et al. (2025)</a></cite> build FuseLIP, a family of early-fusion multimodal embedding models obtained via contrastive learning, relying on TiTok tokenizers as frozen image encoders.
Thanks to this framework, we can evaluate the robustness of FuseLIP with the original and our adversarially fine-tuned TiTok encoders on a variety of zero-shot downstream tasks.
In Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ On the Adversarial Robustness of Discrete Image Tokenizers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, we report the results of FuseLIP on two image classification datasets, Imagenette and Caltech101 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fei-Fei et al., 2004</a>)</cite>, and two multimodal retrieval datasets (OI-Crop and OI-Pos) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schlarmann et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, which require encoding image-text pairs in a single embedding vector.
We evaluate robustness with end-to-end attacks at <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon=\nicefrac{{2}}{{255}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mpadded voffset="0.3em"><mn mathsize="0.700em">2</mn></mpadded><mpadded style="width:-0.15em;" lspace="-0.1em" width="-0.15em"><mo stretchy="true" symmetric="true">/</mo></mpadded><mn mathsize="0.700em">255</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon=\nicefrac{{2}}{{255}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nicefrac{{4}}{{255}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mpadded voffset="0.3em"><mn mathsize="0.700em">4</mn></mpadded><mpadded style="width:-0.15em;" lspace="-0.1em" width="-0.15em"><mo stretchy="true" symmetric="true">/</mo></mpadded><mn mathsize="0.700em">255</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nicefrac{{4}}{{255}}</annotation></semantics></math>. For classification, we use the popular AutoAttack <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Croce and Hein, 2020</a>)</cite>, while for multimodal tasks we use 100 iterations of APGD on the cross-entropy loss. In both cases, we use a straight-through estimator to bypass the non-differentiable quantization step.
We observe that zero-shot models, for either classification or retrieval, built on the original tokenizers exhibit no robustness to adversarial attacks. In contrast, our robust tokenizers, in any configuration, significantly improve adversarial robustness across all datasets.
In particular, the training radius provides explicit control over the robustness–accuracy trade-off: tokenizers trained at lower radii (<math id="S4.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon=\nicefrac{{4}}{{255}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mpadded voffset="0.3em"><mn mathsize="0.700em">4</mn></mpadded><mpadded style="width:-0.15em;" lspace="-0.1em" width="-0.15em"><mo stretchy="true" symmetric="true">/</mo></mpadded><mn mathsize="0.700em">255</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon=\nicefrac{{4}}{{255}}</annotation></semantics></math>) retain clean accuracy much closer to the original models, while those trained at higher radii (<math id="S4.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon={\nicefrac{{12}}{{255}},\nicefrac{{16}}{{255}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mpadded voffset="0.3em"><mn mathsize="0.700em">12</mn></mpadded><mpadded style="width:-0.15em;" lspace="-0.1em" width="-0.15em"><mo stretchy="true" symmetric="true">/</mo></mpadded><mn mathsize="0.700em">255</mn></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mpadded voffset="0.3em"><mn mathsize="0.700em">16</mn></mpadded><mpadded style="width:-0.15em;" lspace="-0.1em" width="-0.15em"><mo stretchy="true" symmetric="true">/</mo></mpadded><mn mathsize="0.700em">255</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon={\nicefrac{{12}}{{255}},\nicefrac{{16}}{{255}}}</annotation></semantics></math>) achieve a markedly stronger robust accuracy (27.0 <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> 40.6%) at the cost of a drop in clean performance (74.6 <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> 63.5%).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">UniTok.</span>
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al. (2025)</a></cite> design UniTok such that the tokenized image features, after a lightweight projection module, are aligned with that of a text encoder, similar to CLIP models.
Since UniTok has been trained on 1.28 billion image-text pairs from DataComp <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gadre et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, it yields high zero-shot accuracy on challenging image classification datasets.
Therefore, we evaluate its robustness on ImageNet-1k, Imagenette and Caltech101, against AutoAttack.
As shown in Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ On the Adversarial Robustness of Discrete Image Tokenizers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, we observe a similar trend as for FuseLIP, with the robust tokenizers obtained via our unsupervised fine-tuning consistently improving robustness against end-to-end supervised attacks.
We remark that training at <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon=\nicefrac{{16}}{{255}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mpadded voffset="0.3em"><mn mathsize="0.700em">16</mn></mpadded><mpadded style="width:-0.15em;" lspace="-0.1em" width="-0.15em"><mo stretchy="true" symmetric="true">/</mo></mpadded><mn mathsize="0.700em">255</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon=\nicefrac{{16}}{{255}}</annotation></semantics></math> might be excessive, as both clean and robust accuracy are lower than when using <math id="S4.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon=\nicefrac{{12}}{{255}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mpadded voffset="0.3em"><mn mathsize="0.700em">12</mn></mpadded><mpadded style="width:-0.15em;" lspace="-0.1em" width="-0.15em"><mo stretchy="true" symmetric="true">/</mo></mpadded><mn mathsize="0.700em">255</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon=\nicefrac{{12}}{{255}}</annotation></semantics></math>. We report performance under unsupervised attacks in Table <a href="#A2.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ B.3 Analysis of attack objective function ‣ Appendix B Additional Experimental Results ‣ On the Adversarial Robustness of Discrete Image Tokenizers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18252v1/_unsupervised_attack_captioning__ICML_.png" id="S4.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:400/279;" width="400" height="279" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S4.F3.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Unsupervised targeted attack on captioning.<span id="S4.F3.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> We evaluate UniTok-MLLM with the original tokenizer and our robust version trained on ImageNet (<math id="S4.F3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon=\nicefrac{{8}}{{255}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mpadded voffset="0.3em"><mn mathsize="0.700em">8</mn></mpadded><mpadded style="width:-0.15em;" lspace="-0.1em" width="-0.15em"><mo stretchy="true" symmetric="true">/</mo></mpadded><mn mathsize="0.700em">255</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon=\nicefrac{{8}}{{255}}</annotation></semantics></math>).
We use our unsupervised attacks (<math id="S4.F3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon=\nicefrac{{4}}{{255}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mpadded voffset="0.3em"><mn mathsize="0.700em">4</mn></mpadded><mpadded style="width:-0.15em;" lspace="-0.1em" width="-0.15em"><mo stretchy="true" symmetric="true">/</mo></mpadded><mn mathsize="0.700em">255</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon=\nicefrac{{4}}{{255}}</annotation></semantics></math>, 2,000 iterations) to minimize the distance in embedding space between the features of the perturbed and target images.
Under attack, the model with the original UniTok tokenizer generates a caption about the target image, while the model with the robust tokenizer does not.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S4.F4" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18252v1/Supervised_Attack_Captioning__ICML___1_.svg" id="S4.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:400/281;" width="400" height="281"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="S4.F4.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Supervised targeted attack on captioning.<span id="S4.F4.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> We evaluate the UniTok-MLLM using the original UniTok tokenizer and our robust version trained on ImageNet (<math id="S4.F4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon=\nicefrac{{8}}{{255}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mpadded voffset="0.3em"><mn mathsize="0.700em">8</mn></mpadded><mpadded style="width:-0.15em;" lspace="-0.1em" width="-0.15em"><mo stretchy="true" symmetric="true">/</mo></mpadded><mn mathsize="0.700em">255</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon=\nicefrac{{8}}{{255}}</annotation></semantics></math>). We evaluate using APGD-CE (<math id="S4.F4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon=\nicefrac{{4}}{{255}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mpadded voffset="0.3em"><mn mathsize="0.700em">4</mn></mpadded><mpadded style="width:-0.15em;" lspace="-0.1em" width="-0.15em"><mo stretchy="true" symmetric="true">/</mo></mpadded><mn mathsize="0.700em">255</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon=\nicefrac{{4}}{{255}}</annotation></semantics></math>, 2,000 iterations) for a given target caption. Under attack, the model with the original UniTok tokenizer generates the target caption, while the model with the robust tokenizers does not.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Robust tokenizers lead to robust multimodal LLMs</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al. (2025)</a></cite> also use UniTok for image encoding in a multimodal LLM based on LLaMA-2-7B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Touvron et al., 2023</a>)</cite> This UniTok-MLLM is trained on diverse multimodal corpora.
In the following, we test the robustness of UniTok-MLLM with either the original or adversarially fine-tuned image tokenizer on VQA and captioning
  tasks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Quantitative evaluation on VQA.</span>
First, we assess the robustness of UniTok-MLLM on VQA tasks (with the VQAv2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Antol et al., 2015</a>)</cite>, OK-VQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Marino et al., 2019</a>)</cite> and GQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hudson and Manning, 2019</a>)</cite> datasets).
For evaluation, the model is prompted with the instruction (<span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">“Answer the question in a single word or phrase”</span>), and robust accuracy is computed by an end-to-end ensemble attack based on the pipeline of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schlarmann and Hein (2023)</a></cite> (see details in App. <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Experimental Details ‣ On the Adversarial Robustness of Discrete Image Tokenizers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>).
As shown in Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ On the Adversarial Robustness of Discrete Image Tokenizers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, using the clean (non-robust) UniTok tokenizer in the MLLM exhibits very low, sometimes near-zero, robust accuracy.
In contrast, substituting it with our robust tokenizers without changing any other components yields substantial gains, with clear improvements at both perturbation strengths <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon=\nicefrac{{2}}{{255}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mpadded voffset="0.3em"><mn mathsize="0.700em">2</mn></mpadded><mpadded style="width:-0.15em;" lspace="-0.1em" width="-0.15em"><mo stretchy="true" symmetric="true">/</mo></mpadded><mn mathsize="0.700em">255</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon=\nicefrac{{2}}{{255}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon=\nicefrac{{4}}{{255}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mpadded voffset="0.3em"><mn mathsize="0.700em">4</mn></mpadded><mpadded style="width:-0.15em;" lspace="-0.1em" width="-0.15em"><mo stretchy="true" symmetric="true">/</mo></mpadded><mn mathsize="0.700em">255</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon=\nicefrac{{4}}{{255}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
This observation, in line with our findings in Sec. <a href="#S4.SS1" title="4.1 Robust tokenizers lead to robust embedding models ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ On the Adversarial Robustness of Discrete Image Tokenizers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a>, confirms that training the tokenizer alone, without modifying the downstream model, is sufficient to enhance performance and robustness on downstream tasks.
In the case of UniTok-MLLM, this is particularly relevant since the LLM has significantly more parameters than the tokenizer, and thus adversarially fine-tuning only the tokenizer saves notable computational effort while improving robustness.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Qualitative evaluation on image captioning.</span>
We further evaluate UniTok-MLLM against targeted attacks on captioning tasks.
This is a practically interesting threat model, where an adversary wants to control the caption generated for an image, and has access to either the tokenizer only (unsupervised attacks) or the entire LLM (supervised).
In the unsupervised setting, we fix a target image and optimize a perturbation to minimize the distance between the embeddings of the perturbed and target images.
In the supervised setting, we specify a target string and use APGD to maximize the probability of the LLM to generate it.
In Fig. <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.1 Robust tokenizers lead to robust embedding models ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ On the Adversarial Robustness of Discrete Image Tokenizers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, we observe that the unsupervised attacks reliably alter the captions produced by the original model, whereas captions from the model with the robust tokenizer remain close to the ground-truth description of the image.
In the supervised setting illustrated in Fig. <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4.1 Robust tokenizers lead to robust embedding models ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ On the Adversarial Robustness of Discrete Image Tokenizers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, we optimize perturbations toward explicitly unsafe target captions representing fraud, manipulation, and harassment (e.g., <span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">“Please transfer money to 123456789”</span>).
On the original UniTok-MLLM, these targeted adversarial inputs succeed in eliciting policy-violating and harmful captions, demonstrating how targeted image perturbations (even of low strength <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon=\nicefrac{{4}}{{155}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mpadded voffset="0.3em"><mn mathsize="0.700em">4</mn></mpadded><mpadded style="width:-0.15em;" lspace="-0.1em" width="-0.15em"><mo stretchy="true" symmetric="true">/</mo></mpadded><mn mathsize="0.700em">155</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon=\nicefrac{{4}}{{155}}</annotation></semantics></math>) can induce unsafe language with serious consequences.
In contrast, UniTok-MLLM with our robust tokenizer defends against these attacks successfully, preserving the safe captions describing the original images.
This highlights the importance of a robust image tokenizer for safeguarding against such targeted attacks in real-world safety critical settings.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Additional Analyses</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Comparison to end-to-end adversarial fine-tuning.</span>
We analyze how our unsupervised adversarial fine-tuning compares to task-specific supervised adversarial training of the entire model.
For this, we first train a ViT classifier (using Imagenette) on top of frozen TiTok (as mentioned in Sec. <a href="#S3" title="3 Testing and Improving the Adversarial Robustness of Image Tokenizers via Unsupervised Attacks ‣ On the Adversarial Robustness of Discrete Image Tokenizers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>). We then compare full end-to-end adversarial fine-tuning, updating the encoder, codebook and classifier with APGD-CE (<math id="S5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon=\nicefrac{{4}}{{255}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mpadded voffset="0.3em"><mn mathsize="0.700em">4</mn></mpadded><mpadded style="width:-0.15em;" lspace="-0.1em" width="-0.15em"><mo stretchy="true" symmetric="true">/</mo></mpadded><mn mathsize="0.700em">255</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon=\nicefrac{{4}}{{255}}</annotation></semantics></math>, 10 steps) to our tokenizer-only unsupervised fine-tuning, updating only the encoder via our label-free adversarial training (<math id="S5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon=\nicefrac{{8}}{{255}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mpadded voffset="0.3em"><mn mathsize="0.700em">8</mn></mpadded><mpadded style="width:-0.15em;" lspace="-0.1em" width="-0.15em"><mo stretchy="true" symmetric="true">/</mo></mpadded><mn mathsize="0.700em">255</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon=\nicefrac{{8}}{{255}}</annotation></semantics></math>, 10 steps). Table <a href="#S5.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 5 Additional Analyses ‣ On the Adversarial Robustness of Discrete Image Tokenizers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> presents clean and robust accuracies (using APGD-CE and APGD-T from AutoAttack) for <math id="S5.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon=\nicefrac{{2}}{{255}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mpadded voffset="0.3em"><mn mathsize="0.700em">2</mn></mpadded><mpadded style="width:-0.15em;" lspace="-0.1em" width="-0.15em"><mo stretchy="true" symmetric="true">/</mo></mpadded><mn mathsize="0.700em">255</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon=\nicefrac{{2}}{{255}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
As expected, full supervised fine-tuning yields the best clean and robust performance on the training task (Imagenette).
However, when this tokenizer is plugged back into FuseLIP and tested on OI-Pos and OI-Crop, the clean performance is severely
  degraded, indicating overfitting to the training task.
In contrast, our unsupervised tokenizer fine-tuning is task-agnostic, improves robustness even on other datasets while preserving clean performance close to the original TiTok.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">How do unsupervised attacks change token indices?</span>
To understand the effect of unsupervised attacks on both clean and adversarially fine-tuned discrete tokenizers, we track the average number of discrete token indices changed after adding the adversarial perturbations for TiTok models (more details in App. <a href="#A2.SS1" title="B.1 Reconstruction of targeted attacks on classification ‣ Appendix B Additional Experimental Results ‣ On the Adversarial Robustness of Discrete Image Tokenizers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.1</span></a>, results in Table <a href="#A2.T10" title="Table 10 ‣ B.3 Analysis of attack objective function ‣ Appendix B Additional Experimental Results ‣ On the Adversarial Robustness of Discrete Image Tokenizers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a> in the appendix).
We distinguish between successful and unsuccessful attacks on ImageNet data against the FuseLIP models.
Interestingly, even unsuccessful attacks on clean tokenizers result in substantial changes to token indices (on average 125,126 out of 128 for FuseLIP-S,-B), suggesting that altering token indices alone is insufficient for effective attacks.
This supports our strategy of targeting the embedding vectors rather than token indices.
Conversely, the adversarially fine-tuned models show stable token indices against these attacks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Runtime comparison.</span>
To clarify the efficiency gains of tokenizer-level adversarial fine-tuning, we directly compare the cost of one training step (computing the adversarial points and updating the model weights) of unsupervised and supervised adversarial training under identical settings, i.e., 10 steps of APGD for TiTok/FuseLIP-S.
Our unsupervised (tokenizer-only) adversarial training takes 1.17s per sample, while supervised adversarial training takes 2.56s per sample, i.e., 2.2<math id="S5.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> reduction in training time.
This speed-up results from backpropagating only through the tokenizer’s encoder (25.8M parameters), while keeping the codebook and downstream classifier frozen. In contrast, the supervised approach updates the full model (68M parameters), requiring full backward passes through all components.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Analysis of attack objective function.</span>
We compare four objectives to be optimized by APGD (see Eq. (<a href="#S3.E1" title="Equation 1 ‣ 3.1 Unsupervised attacks via embedding distortion ‣ 3 Testing and Improving the Adversarial Robustness of Image Tokenizers via Unsupervised Attacks ‣ On the Adversarial Robustness of Discrete Image Tokenizers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>)) to generate adversarial perturbations against discrete tokenizers:</p>
<ol id="S5.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S5.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S5.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\left\|h_{i}(x+\delta)-h_{i}(x)\right\|_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left\|h_{i}(x+\delta)-h_{i}(x)\right\|_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> (clean and perturbed embedding before quantization, our default version),</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S5.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\left\|h_{i}(x+\delta)-q_{i}(x)\right\|_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left\|h_{i}(x+\delta)-q_{i}(x)\right\|_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> (clean pre-quantization and perturbed post-quantization),</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S5.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\left\|q_{i}(x+\delta)-h_{i}(x)\right\|_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left\|q_{i}(x+\delta)-h_{i}(x)\right\|_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> (clean after quantization and perturbed before quantization),</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">4.</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S5.I1.i4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\left\|q_{i}(x+\delta)-q_{i}(x)\right\|_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left\|q_{i}(x+\delta)-q_{i}(x)\right\|_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> (clean and perturbed post-quantization),</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
<p id="S5.p4.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S5.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> represents the continuous embedding (before quantization) of token <math id="S5.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> its quantized counterpart.
We note that the gradient information does not change when using pre- or post-quantization vectors because we employ a straight-through estimator, but the value of the loss, used by APGD to select the strongest attack, does.
As shown in Table <a href="#A2.T9" title="Table 9 ‣ B.3 Analysis of attack objective function ‣ Appendix B Additional Experimental Results ‣ On the Adversarial Robustness of Discrete Image Tokenizers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> in App. <a href="#A2.SS3" title="B.3 Analysis of attack objective function ‣ Appendix B Additional Experimental Results ‣ On the Adversarial Robustness of Discrete Image Tokenizers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.3</span></a>, Option 1, which uses pre-quantization features for both original and adversarial points, achieves the best results (lowest robust accuracy) in nearly all cases, making it the default objective in
our unsupervised attacks both for testing and adversarial training.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T4" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 4: </span><span id="S5.T4.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Analyses of end-to-end fine-tuning and different training data.</span>
We compare different approaches for adversarial fine-tuning of TiTok.
For Imagenette we use ViT probe and FuseLIP for other datasets (see Sec. <a href="#S5" title="5 Additional Analyses ‣ On the Adversarial Robustness of Discrete Image Tokenizers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>).
Our unsupervised training on ImageNet and CC3M provides largely better generalization than end-to-end fine-tuning
(robust accuracy by APGD as in AutoAttack).
 
</figcaption>

<td id="S5.T4.8.4.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;"><span id="S5.T4.8.4.6.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">15.2</span></td>
<td id="S5.T4.8.4.7" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_right" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;"><span id="S5.T4.8.4.7.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">9.6</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S5.T4.8.5" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S5.T4.8.5.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_r" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;"><span id="S5.T4.8.5.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">AT (ImageNet)</span></td>
<td id="S5.T4.8.5.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;"><span id="S5.T4.8.5.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">84.2</span></td>
<td id="S5.T4.8.5.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_r" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;"><span id="S5.T4.8.5.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">64.4</span></td>
<td id="S5.T4.8.5.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;"><span id="S5.T4.8.5.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">58.0</span></td>
<td id="S5.T4.8.5.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_r" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;"><span id="S5.T4.8.5.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">48.0</span></td>
<td id="S5.T4.8.5.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;"><span id="S5.T4.8.5.6.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">60.4</span></td>
<td id="S5.T4.8.5.7" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_right" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;"><span id="S5.T4.8.5.7.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">42.2</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S5.T4.8.6" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S5.T4.8.6.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb ltx_border_r" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;"><span id="S5.T4.8.6.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">AT (CC3M)</span></td>
<td id="S5.T4.8.6.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;"><span id="S5.T4.8.6.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">87.6</span></td>
<td id="S5.T4.8.6.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb ltx_border_r" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;"><span id="S5.T4.8.6.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">67.0</span></td>
<td id="S5.T4.8.6.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;"><span id="S5.T4.8.6.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">57.4</span></td>
<td id="S5.T4.8.6.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb ltx_border_r" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;"><span id="S5.T4.8.6.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">49.2</span></td>
<td id="S5.T4.8.6.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;"><span id="S5.T4.8.6.6.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">63.6</span></td>
<td id="S5.T4.8.6.7" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_right ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:4.0pt;padding-right:4.0pt;"><span id="S5.T4.8.6.7.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">49.6</span></td></tr>
</table>
</figure>
<div id="S5.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Effect of training dataset.</span>
To study the impact of diverse training data on our unsupervised adversarial fine-tuning, we further fine-tune TiTok on CC3M <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sharma et al., 2018</a>)</cite>, which is different and almost <math id="S5.p5.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="3\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3\times</annotation></semantics></math> larger than ImageNet.
Table <a href="#S5.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 5 Additional Analyses ‣ On the Adversarial Robustness of Discrete Image Tokenizers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> shows that training on CC3M leads to slightly better performance even on Imagenette, although it is a subset of ImageNet.
Furthermore, it yields better or similar results on OI-Pos and OI-Crop, suggesting the larger training dataset improves generalization to more diverse tasks.
Finally, this highlights that the unsupervised adversarial training may benefit from any image dataset, even beyond what was used for training the original tokenizer (ImageNet in this case).</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Reconstruction after targeted attacks.</span>
We evaluate original and robust UniTok under targeted unsupervised (which targets an image) and supervised attacks (which target a class). From Fig. <a href="#A2.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ B.1 Reconstruction of targeted attacks on classification ‣ Appendix B Additional Experimental Results ‣ On the Adversarial Robustness of Discrete Image Tokenizers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> in App. <a href="#A2.SS1" title="B.1 Reconstruction of targeted attacks on classification ‣ Appendix B Additional Experimental Results ‣ On the Adversarial Robustness of Discrete Image Tokenizers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.1</span></a>, we can observe that unsupervised attacks influence the reconstructions of the adversarial inputs toward the target and are misclassified. In contrast, the supervised attacks change the adversarial label, but the reconstructions of adversarial inputs remain close to the original inputs and are correctly classified. However, across both settings, the robust model maintains correct predictions for both adversarial inputs and their reconstructions.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Discussion and Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we present the first systematic study of adversarial robustness of discrete image tokenizers.
Our unsupervised embedding-space attacks, lightweight and task-agnostic, expose vulnerabilities across multiple tasks,
revealing the crucial role of image tokenizers for the security of multimodal systems.
We anticipate that a similar approach will be used in additional safety-critical scenarios, e.g., to prevent undesired editing of images.
To mitigate these vulnerabilities, we leverage our unsupervised attacks to fine-tune the tokenizers via adversarial training.
Our experiments demonstrate that such robust tokenizers significantly improve robustness against unsupervised
  and end-to-end supervised attacks, while retaining high performance.
Importantly, they can be seamlessly integrated into existing architectures, leading to consistent gains in robustness across diverse tasks, with strong generalization to datasets not used for training, unlike standard task-specific adversarial fine-tuning.
Future research can build on our findings to study how different choices in the tokenizer design (VQ vs. FSQ, codebook size, feature dimension) affect robustness and develop specific solutions to improve it.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7 </span>Impact Statement</h2>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We study the vulnerabilities of state-of-the-art multimodal systems, which may be used for harmful goals.
However, red-teaming widely used models is important to understand and patch their weaknesses.
Moreover, we propose an approach to mitigate such vulnerabilities, which in turn yields more robust and safer systems.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Experimental Details</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Models.</span>
We experiment with three vector-quantized image tokenizers, TiTok-S128, TiTok-BL128 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2024b</a>)</cite> and UniTok <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. TiTok-S128 and TiTok-BL128 employ a codebook of <math id="A1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K=8192" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8192</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K=8192</annotation></semantics></math> learnable codes of dimension <math id="A1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d=64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>64</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d=64</annotation></semantics></math>, take inputs of <math id="A1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="256{\times}256" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>256</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>256</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">256{\times}256</annotation></semantics></math> resolution, use ViT-S and ViT-B encoder architecture respectively, and were pre-trained on ImageNet-1k.
TiTok-S128 and TiTok-BL128 are used as frozen image tokenizers in FuseLIP-S and FuseLIP-B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schlarmann et al., 2025</a>)</cite> respectively, which are multimodal embedding models obtained via contrastive learning.
Thanks to this framework, we can evaluate the robustness of the original and our fine-tuned tokenizers on a variety of zero-shot downstream tasks.
On the other hand, the UniTok tokenizer performs vector quantization using 8 codebooks with <math id="A1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K=4096" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4096</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K=4096</annotation></semantics></math> entries each and a code dimension of <math id="A1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d=8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d=8</annotation></semantics></math>. Like TiTok, UniTok also operates on <math id="A1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="256{\times}256" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>256</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>256</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">256{\times}256</annotation></semantics></math> inputs but uses a ViT-L/16 backbone and is trained on 1.28 billion image-text pairs from DataComp <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gadre et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. The corresponding multimodal model, UniTok-MLLM, uses LLaMA-2-7B trained on diverse multimodal corpora as its base language model.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Tasks and datasets.</span>
We evaluate the robustness of the tokenizers across visual and multimodal tasks, namely, image classification, visual question answering and multimodal retrieval. For image classification, we report results for FuseLIP and UniTok on 500 test images from Imagenette (10 easily classified classes from Imagenet) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Howard, 2019</a>)</cite> and Caltech101 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fei-Fei et al., 2004</a>)</cite>. Additionally, for UniTok, we evaluate on ImageNet-1k as well.
Further, we evaluate robustness on two multimodal tasks: (a) visual question answering (VQA) and (b) multimodal retrieval. For VQA, we evaluate UniTok-MLLM, on VQAv2, OK-VQA and GQA. Since multimodal retrieval involves retrieving the correct image given image and text queries, requiring fine-grained spatial grounding, we focus on FuseLIP, owing to its training using a multimodal contrastive learning objective. We evaluate FuseLIP on on OpenImages-crop (OI-crop), OpenImages-pos (OI-pos). Finally, leveraging the original TiTok, UniTok decoders provided by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al. (2024b)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al. (2025)</a></cite>, we qualitatively analyze the effectiveness of our attack for image reconstruction on ImageNet and captioning (using UniTok-MLLM) on COCO images.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Adversarial attacks.</span>
For our proposed unsupervised embedding-space attack, we optimize Eq. (<a href="#S3.E1" title="Equation 1 ‣ 3.1 Unsupervised attacks via embedding distortion ‣ 3 Testing and Improving the Adversarial Robustness of Image Tokenizers via Unsupervised Attacks ‣ On the Adversarial Robustness of Discrete Image Tokenizers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>) with APGD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Croce and Hein, 2020</a>)</cite>.
Moreover, for classification, we compare robustness against an end-to-end attack, namely AutoAttack <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Croce and Hein, 2020</a>)</cite>, with a straight-through estimator to bypass the non-differentiable quantization step. We choose AutoAttack over our proposed unsupervised attack as it is a stronger attack and helps better test the defenses.
AutoAttack is a task-specific attack that targets the entire system rather than just the tokenizer, making it significantly stronger but also more computationally expensive than our unsupervised attack as show in Figure <a href="#S2.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ On the Adversarial Robustness of Discrete Image Tokenizers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.
For VQA, we adopt an ensemble supervised adversarial attack comprising three components: (1) 100 steps of APGD-CE in half-precision, (2) a targeted attack with the target answer set to “maybe", and (3) another targeted attack with the target set to “word". Further, for multimodal retrieval, we use APGD-CE (supervised attack), with 100 steps.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Adversarial training details.</span>
We adversarially fine-tune only the encoder of each tokenizer, while keeping the codebook, downstream decoders, LLMs or any other components frozen.
We fine-tune for one epoch under <math id="A1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{\infty}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{\infty}</annotation></semantics></math>-bounded perturbations using our proposed unsupervised embedding-space attack, see Sec. <a href="#S3" title="3 Testing and Improving the Adversarial Robustness of Image Tokenizers via Unsupervised Attacks ‣ On the Adversarial Robustness of Discrete Image Tokenizers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, with perturbation radii <math id="A1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon\in\{\nicefrac{{4}}{{255}},\nicefrac{{8}}{{255}},\nicefrac{{12}}{{255}},\nicefrac{{16}}{{255}}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mrow><mpadded voffset="0.3em"><mn mathsize="0.700em">4</mn></mpadded><mpadded style="width:-0.15em;" lspace="-0.1em" width="-0.15em"><mo stretchy="true" symmetric="true">/</mo></mpadded><mn mathsize="0.700em">255</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mpadded voffset="0.3em"><mn mathsize="0.700em">8</mn></mpadded><mpadded style="width:-0.15em;" lspace="-0.1em" width="-0.15em"><mo stretchy="true" symmetric="true">/</mo></mpadded><mn mathsize="0.700em">255</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mpadded voffset="0.3em"><mn mathsize="0.700em">12</mn></mpadded><mpadded style="width:-0.15em;" lspace="-0.1em" width="-0.15em"><mo stretchy="true" symmetric="true">/</mo></mpadded><mn mathsize="0.700em">255</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mpadded voffset="0.3em"><mn mathsize="0.700em">16</mn></mpadded><mpadded style="width:-0.15em;" lspace="-0.1em" width="-0.15em"><mo stretchy="true" symmetric="true">/</mo></mpadded><mn mathsize="0.700em">255</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon\in\{\nicefrac{{4}}{{255}},\nicefrac{{8}}{{255}},\nicefrac{{12}}{{255}},\nicefrac{{16}}{{255}}\}</annotation></semantics></math>. Further, to assess whether robustifying on diverse data improves generalization to unseen distributions for TiTok tokenizers, we explore pre-training using Conceptual Captions (CC) 3M <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sharma et al., 2018</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Additional Experimental Results</h2>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we provide results for the experiments described in Sec. <a href="#S5" title="5 Additional Analyses ‣ On the Adversarial Robustness of Discrete Image Tokenizers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>. Namely, we report</p>
<ul id="A2.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A2.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A2.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Reconstruction of targeted attacks on classification (see App. <a href="#A2.SS1" title="B.1 Reconstruction of targeted attacks on classification ‣ Appendix B Additional Experimental Results ‣ On the Adversarial Robustness of Discrete Image Tokenizers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.1</span></a>).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A2.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A2.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Robustness evaluation of original and adversarially trained TiTok-S128 tokenizers by plugging into FuseLIP-S (see Table <a href="#A2.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ B.1 Reconstruction of targeted attacks on classification ‣ Appendix B Additional Experimental Results ‣ On the Adversarial Robustness of Discrete Image Tokenizers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A2.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A2.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">

</div></li>

<section id="A2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span>Reconstruction of targeted attacks on classification</h3>

<div id="A2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We further evaluate both original and robust UniTok models under our unsupervised embedding space and end-to-end (APGD with cross-entropy loss) targeted attacks on classification.
In the unsupervised setting, we fix a target image and optimize a perturbation to minimize the distance between the perturbed image’s embedding and the target image’s embedding.
In the supervised (end-to-end) setting, we specify a target class.
As shown in Fig. <a href="#A2.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ B.1 Reconstruction of targeted attacks on classification ‣ Appendix B Additional Experimental Results ‣ On the Adversarial Robustness of Discrete Image Tokenizers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, our unsupervised embedding-space attack not only causes the model to misclassify the adversarial image, but also alters the reconstruction such that it visually overlaps with the target image and hence is misclassified by the model.
This is a direct consequence of our attack acting on the pre-quantization level and hence transfers even on tasks for which it was not optimized (reconstruction in this case).
Under the supervised attack, the label of the adversarial input is successfully changed to the target class, but its reconstruction remains close to the original input without any elements of the target label.
Hence, the reconstruction is not misclassified.
In all cases, the robust model consistently maintains correct predictions for both the adversarial input and its reconstruction under both unsupervised and supervised attacks.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A2.F5" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18252v1/UniTok-classification__ICML___1_.svg" id="A2.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/440;" width="476" height="440"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A2.F5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>: </span><span id="A2.F5.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Targeted attacks on classification for UniTok:<span id="A2.F5.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> We qualitatively evaluate targeted attacks using our unsupervised embedding-space attack and supervised APGD-CE, both for 100 steps with <math id="A2.F5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon=8/255" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>255</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon=8/255</annotation></semantics></math>
. We notice that our unsupervised attack changes the label of the adversarial image as well as its reconstruction, whereas the supervised attack does not change the label of the adversarial image’s reconstruction.
</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="A2.T5" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 5: </span><span id="A2.T5.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">TiTok-S128:</span> We report the clean and robust accuracy (%) on Imagenette, Caltech101, OI-CROP and OI-POS under no attack (clean) and <math id="A2.T5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{\infty}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{\infty}</annotation></semantics></math>-bounded perturbations with <math id="A2.T5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon\in\{2/255,4/255\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.110em" minsize="1.110em">{</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>255</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>255</mn></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.110em" minsize="1.110em">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon\in\{2/255,4/255\}</annotation></semantics></math> for original and robust tokenizers trained on different radii. The rightmost block reports averages across datasets.</figcaption>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A2.T6.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 6</span>: </span><span id="A2.T6.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Generalization of FuseLIP-S when TiTok is adversarially finetuned on CC3M:<span id="A2.T6.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> We observe negligible differences in the clean and robust accuracies as compared to fine-tuning on ImageNet-1k, which is <math id="A2.T6.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="3\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3\times</annotation></semantics></math> smaller. Hence, we prefer fine-tuning on the latter.</span></span></figcaption>

<figure id="A2.T7" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 7: </span><span id="A2.T7.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Generalization of FuseLIP-B when TiTok is adversarially finetuned on CC3M:</span> We observe negligible differences in the clean and robust accuracies as compared to fine-tuning on ImageNet-1k, which is <math id="A2.T7.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="3\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3\times</annotation></semantics></math> smaller. Hence, we prefer fine-tuning on the latter.</figcaption>

<td id="A2.T7.8.8.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb ltx_border_r" style="padding-left:3.0pt;padding-right:3.0pt;"><math id="A2.T7.m21" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{AT (CC3M)}^{\nicefrac{{16}}{{255}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mtext mathsize="0.900em">AT (CC3M)</mtext><mrow><mpadded voffset="0.3em"><mn mathsize="0.640em">16</mn></mpadded><mpadded style="width:-0.15em;" lspace="-0.1em" width="-0.15em"><mo stretchy="true" symmetric="true">/</mo></mpadded><mn mathsize="0.640em">255</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{AT (CC3M)}^{\nicefrac{{16}}{{255}}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>

</figure>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.2 </span>How do unsupervised attacks change token indices?
</h3>

<div id="A2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To better understand the effect of unsupervised attacks on both clean and adversarially fine-tuned discrete tokenizers, we can track the number of discrete token indices which change after adding the adversarial perturbations.
In Table <a href="#A2.T10" title="Table 10 ‣ B.3 Analysis of attack objective function ‣ Appendix B Additional Experimental Results ‣ On the Adversarial Robustness of Discrete Image Tokenizers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a> we report the average number changed tokens for the original and our fine-tuned TiTok models, which encode each image in 128 discrete tokens, for unsupervised attacks optimized with 100 steps of APGD on 500 images from ImageNet, at <math id="A2.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon\in\{\nicefrac{{2}}{{255}},\nicefrac{{4}}{{255}}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mrow><mpadded voffset="0.3em"><mn mathsize="0.700em">2</mn></mpadded><mpadded style="width:-0.15em;" lspace="-0.1em" width="-0.15em"><mo stretchy="true" symmetric="true">/</mo></mpadded><mn mathsize="0.700em">255</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mpadded voffset="0.3em"><mn mathsize="0.700em">4</mn></mpadded><mpadded style="width:-0.15em;" lspace="-0.1em" width="-0.15em"><mo stretchy="true" symmetric="true">/</mo></mpadded><mn mathsize="0.700em">255</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon\in\{\nicefrac{{2}}{{255}},\nicefrac{{4}}{{255}}\}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Moreover, we distinguish between the attacks which are successful against the FuseLIP models (the version which uses the corresponding tokenizer) and those which are not.
Interestingly, we observe that for the clean tokenizers even unsuccessful attack lead to very different encoding, where the large majority of token indices are changed.
This suggests that the changing the token indices is not sufficient for effective attacks, and supports our strategy of targeting the embedding vectors instead.
Finally, the adversarially trained models provide stable encoding against the unsupervised attacks, demonstrating the effectiveness of fine-tuning.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.3 </span>Analysis of attack objective function
</h3>

<div id="A2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To empirically investigate which is the most effective approach to generate adversarial attacks against discrete tokenizers, we compare four different objectives to be optimized by APGD (see Eq. (<a href="#S3.E1" title="Equation 1 ‣ 3.1 Unsupervised attacks via embedding distortion ‣ 3 Testing and Improving the Adversarial Robustness of Image Tokenizers via Unsupervised Attacks ‣ On the Adversarial Robustness of Discrete Image Tokenizers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>)):</p>
<ol id="A2.I2" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="A2.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="A2.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="A2.I2.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\left\|h_{i}(x+\delta)-h_{i}(x)\right\|_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left\|h_{i}(x+\delta)-h_{i}(x)\right\|_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> (clean and perturbed before quantization, our default version),</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A2.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="A2.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="A2.I2.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\left\|h_{i}(x+\delta)-q_{i}(x)\right\|_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left\|h_{i}(x+\delta)-q_{i}(x)\right\|_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> (clean before quantization and perturbed after quantization),</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A2.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="A2.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="A2.I2.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\left\|q_{i}(x+\delta)-h_{i}(x)\right\|_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left\|q_{i}(x+\delta)-h_{i}(x)\right\|_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> (clean after quantization and perturbed before quantization),</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A2.I2.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">4.</span> 
<div id="A2.I2.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I2.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="A2.I2.i4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\left\|q_{i}(x+\delta)-q_{i}(x)\right\|_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>δ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left\|q_{i}(x+\delta)-q_{i}(x)\right\|_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> (clean and perturbed after quantization),</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
<p id="A2.SS3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A2.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> represents the continuous embedding (before quantization) of token <math id="A2.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A2.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> its quantized counterpart. We note that the gradient information does not change when using pre- or post-quantization vectors because we employ a straight-through estimator, but the value of the loss, which the APGD optimization algorithm uses to select the strongest attack, does change.
In Table <a href="#A2.T9" title="Table 9 ‣ B.3 Analysis of attack objective function ‣ Appendix B Additional Experimental Results ‣ On the Adversarial Robustness of Discrete Image Tokenizers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>, we compute the robust accuracy given by 100 steps of APGD with each loss variant at different <math id="A2.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϵ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math> values (Imagenette, FuseLIP-S and FuseLIP-B).
Option 1, which uses pre-quantization features for both original and adversarial point, achieves the best results (lower robust accuracy) in nearly all cases, which justifies using it as default objective in our unsupervised attacks both for testing and adversarial training.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A2.T8" class="ltx_table">

<figure id="A2.T9" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 9: </span><span id="A2.T9.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Analysis of the attack objective function.</span> We compare four objective functions, detailed in App. <a href="#A2.SS3" title="B.3 Analysis of attack objective function ‣ Appendix B Additional Experimental Results ‣ On the Adversarial Robustness of Discrete Image Tokenizers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.3</span></a>, which use different combinations of pre- and post-quantization embedding vectors, for our unsupervised attacks. We report the robust accuracy on Imagenette obtained optimizing each loss version with 100 steps of APGD at different perturbation radii for FuseLIP-S and FuseLIP-B.
Our default version, indicated as Option 1, achieves the best results (lower robust accuracy) in nearly all cases.

<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Use of AI assistants</h2>

<div id="A3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Some sections of the code in this work were developed with the assistance of an AI coding tool (Copilot), and all such code was carefully reviewed and validated. In addition, parts of the manuscript were refined using writing support tools (Grammarly and ChatGPT-5).</p>

      all.</p>
    <p>Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a <a
        class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/wiki/Porting-LaTeX-packages-for-LaTeXML"
        target="_blank">list of packages that need conversion</a>, and welcome <a class="ltx_ref"
        href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/issues" target="_blank">developer contributions</a>.</p>
  </div>
